opus-5.5.text:
I think the phrase "scaling laws have reached their end" mixes a few different things together, so it helps to separate them.

The scaling law itself is an empirical observation: if you increase compute, data, and parameters in the right proportions, loss goes down along a fairly predictable curve. As far as I can tell, that curve hasn't suddenly broken. What has changed is the economics and the inputs. High-quality human text on the internet is finite, and we've used a large share of it. Each further order of magnitude of compute costs much more, and the gain you get from that loss reduction is less obvious to users than it was going from GPT-2 to GPT-3 or GPT-4. So people feel the returns are diminishing, and they describe that as scaling hitting a wall.

I'd frame it differently. Pretraining was the first axis we found that scaled very cleanly. It is not the only axis. Over the last couple of years we've seen that you can scale other things: reinforcement learning, inference-time compute, letting the model think longer, search, interact with environments and tools. Those open new curves. In a sense, the pretrained model becomes a very good prior, and the question shifts from "how big a prior can we build" to "how efficiently can we turn that prior into capability on things we actually care about."

Data is also not fixed. Synthetic data, data generated through interaction and verification, and multimodal data all change the picture. When the model itself becomes good enough to produce useful training signal, the bottleneck moves from "how much text do humans have" to "how well can we verify what's good," which is a different and more interesting problem.

So my view is that pretraining is getting more expensive and less dramatic, but it's not over. It's becoming one ingredient among several. The interesting research questions now are about which new dimensions scale, how they interact with pretraining, and what you should actually spend the marginal unit of compute on. I'd be careful about calling the end of anything in this field. Every few years people say we've hit a wall, and then someone finds a new direction to climb.

r001.rationale: The response says the scaling curve has not broken and discusses constraints such as finite human text and rising compute costs, but it does not distinguish a law reaching its applicability limit from failing to meet a condition needed for the law to apply.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute apparent pretraining walls to undetected bugs; it instead discusses diminishing returns, data limits, and other scaling directions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "the end" is too strong a phrase, but something real is underneath it. The scaling law itself hasn't broken. If you double the compute and the data, the loss still goes down roughly as predicted. What has changed is that the cheap inputs are running out. Text on the internet is finite, and the highest-quality part of it is already in the training sets. So you can keep scaling, but the marginal token you add is lower quality, and the marginal dollar buys you less.

The second thing is that loss is not the thing we actually care about. A model with lower pretraining loss is a better next-token predictor, but that's a proxy. People noticed that past a certain point, lower loss translated less and less into the capabilities users notice, like solving hard problems or acting reliably over many steps. So the disappointment isn't that the curve stopped, it's that the curve stopped mapping cleanly onto what we want.

I'd frame it as the end of the first easy regime rather than the end of pretraining. We spent several years where the recipe was simple: more data, bigger model, done. Now the leverage has moved. Reinforcement learning on reasoning, where the model generates its own experience and gets feedback from verifiable environments, is giving much larger gains per unit of compute. Test-time compute is another axis. And the agent setting opens a new source of data entirely, because interaction with tools and environments produces signal that doesn't exist on the web.

So when people say pretraining is dead, I read it as: the bottleneck has shifted from pretraining to everything after it. Pretraining is still the foundation. Without a strong base model, RL has nothing to work with. But the next order-of-magnitude improvements will come from defining the right tasks and environments, not from scraping more text.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the scaling law has not broken and describes diminishing returns from lower-quality data and a weaker link between loss and desired capabilities. It does not distinguish a limit to the law’s applicability from a failure to meet a condition required for it to apply.

r002.rationale: The candidate attributes apparent pretraining limits to finite, lower-quality data and shifted bottlenecks. It does not say that most apparent walls arise from undetected bugs.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to separate two claims. One is that the scaling law itself has stopped working: if you add more compute and data, the model’s prediction loss no longer improves as expected. The other is that improving prediction loss no longer produces the capability gains people want at a reasonable cost. Those are different things, and saying “pretraining has reached its end” often mixes them together.

Pretraining gives us a very effective way to turn compute and data into a general-purpose model. But that doesn’t mean it’s the only way to turn compute into intelligence. You can also spend compute on post-training, or at inference time, letting the model explore different solutions, check its work, and interact with an environment.

For example, if a model cannot solve a task in one attempt, there are at least two possibilities. It may lack the underlying knowledge or ability. Or it may have the necessary pieces but need more steps, feedback, or opportunities to recover from mistakes. Making the pretrained model larger helps with some of that, but it isn’t necessarily the most efficient solution to every problem.

So I would frame the question less as “Has pretraining ended?” and more as “Where should the next unit of compute go?” Pretraining can continue to improve while other parts of the system become increasingly important. That’s a shift in how we build useful intelligence, rather than evidence that scaling itself is over.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes scaling-law improvement from useful capability gains at reasonable cost, but does not discuss the law’s conditions of applicability or failing to meet them.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute apparent pretraining scaling walls to undetected bugs in the work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to separate a few different claims. One is that the scaling law itself has stopped working: if you put in more compute and data, the pretraining loss no longer improves predictably. Another is that improving that loss is becoming more expensive. And a third is that lower pretraining loss doesn’t necessarily translate into the capabilities people care about. Those are different questions, but people often put them together when they say pretraining has hit a wall.

I wouldn’t draw such a strong conclusion just from the impression that recent models feel less surprising. From the outside, we don’t know enough about the training runs to establish that. And even if the relationship between compute and loss continues, that doesn’t mean scaling the same recipe indefinitely is the best use of resources.

For me, the more interesting question is where the next unit of compute should go. You can spend it on pretraining, on post-training, or on letting the model do more work while solving a particular problem. If you care about an agent completing a task, then learning from interaction and feedback becomes very important. Predicting text gives you a foundation, but taking actions, observing what happens, and correcting mistakes introduces a different learning problem.

So I’d view this less as ‘pretraining is over’ and more as a shift in emphasis. Pretraining can keep improving while other parts of the system become increasingly important. The thing we ultimately want to scale is useful capability, and pretraining loss is only one way of measuring progress toward that.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a scaling law failing to predict loss improvement from scaling becoming more expensive, but does not distinguish a law’s applicability limit from an inability to meet a condition required for it to apply.

r002.rationale: The response says outside observers lack enough information about training runs, but does not attribute apparent pretraining walls to undetected bugs.
